screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contracts
screens.subtitle: Using Web3.js and Ethers.js to connect frontends to Ethereum

narration.text: In this lesson we'll make smart contracts usable by people. Smart contracts live on the blockchain, and your regular web code can't call them directly. JavaScript libraries such as Web3. js and Ethers. js act as a bridge, letting a browser request accounts, read stored values, send signed transactions, and listen for contract events. You'll learn how to choose and configure a provider, obtain a signer for state-changing calls, and create a contract instance from a contract address and its ABI. We'll also practice reading a value with a view function and sending a transaction that changes state. Throughout, I will point out common mistakes like using a provider when a signer is required, missing await on asynchronous calls, or using the wrong ABI. By the end you'll understand why a provider is essential, what a signer does, and how events allow your UI to react to on-chain activity. Think about a simple counter contract: being able to read its current count instantly and let users increment it after confirming a signed transaction is the practical goal of these patterns. How would you design error handling for a user who cancels a transaction?

keyIdea.title: Bridge between web and blockchain
keyIdea.text: Web3.js and Ethers.js let frontends read contract data, send signed transactions, and react to events using a provider and optional signer.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Interacting with Smart Contracts

Interacting with Smart Contracts

Learn the practical steps to connect a browser DApp to Ethereum, instantiate contracts with address and ABI, call read-only functions, and send transactions that modify state.

In this lesson

Why libraries like Ethers.js matter, how providers and signers work, and how to wire a Counter contract from the browser.

Coming up

Hands-on code examples showing read-only calls, transactions, and listening for events with clear debugging tips.

Explore Key Topics

MetaMask or Infura give your DApp access to a node endpoint and user accounts.

Contract Instantiation

Address + ABI create a typed contract object you can call from JavaScript.

Calls vs Transactions

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you should reach four practical skills. First, you will be able to explain why Web3. js or Ethers. js sits between a browser and a blockchain node and what responsibilities the library carries. For example, you will describe how a library encodes function calls and decodes responses. Second, you will be able to configure a JavaScript environment to connect to an Ethereum node using a provider such as MetaMask for browser-based use or Infura for hosted nodes. This includes requesting account access and handling account changes. These skills matter because they turn a compiled smart contract into an interactive web feature a user can operate. You will also learn to recognize common misconceptions, such as assuming a provider can sign transactions, which it cannot without a signer. Finally, you will practice concrete examples that show how to request accounts and create a provider instance so you can move directly to implementing a simple DApp.

keyIdea.title: Four practical outcomes
keyIdea.text: Explain libraries, connect providers, instantiate contracts, and distinguish read-only calls from transactions.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.subtitle: How we will practice these objectives in code

narration.text: This page explains the practical skills you'll practice in the hands-on activity. First, you'll configure MetaMask and request account access from the browser so your DApp can obtain a signer. Then you'll copy the deployed Counter contract address and ABI from Remix and instantiate the contract in JavaScript. This will let you call a view function to read the count and send signed transactions to increment or decrement the counter. During practice you'll observe MetaMask's transaction confirmation flow and learn to await transaction receipts before updating UI state. We'll also show how to listen for a DataChanged or Transfer event so your UI updates without polling. These exercises matter because they mirror real DApp workflows: obtaining a provider, creating a contract object, distinguishing read-only vs state-changing calls, and handling events and errors. By the end you'll be able to wire a simple frontend to a deployed contract and debug common issues.

keyIdea.title: Practice-focused objectives
keyIdea.text: Connect MetaMask, instantiate a contract, execute read and write operations, and listen for events in a DApp workflow.

screens.title: Web3.js vs Ethers.js
screens.subtitle: How both libraries serve as the bridge and where they differ

narration.text: Both Web3. js and Ethers. js provide an A P I to interact with Ethereum from JavaScript, but they present different ergonomics that matter in practice. Ethers. js is commonly chosen for its smaller bundle size, a cleaner, promise-first A P I, and straightforward wallet integration. Web3. js offers a mature feature set with broader historical usage, but it can be heavier in build size and sometimes more complex to configure. Concretely, when I create a contract instance with Ethers. js I typically pass a provider or a signer and call contract methods directly. With Web3. js there are equivalent constructs, but the instantiation and ABI encoding have different helper methods. A common misconception is that one library is strictly more capable; in truth both can do the same tasks of reading state, sending transactions, and subscribing to events. The practical criteria are bundle size, A P I clarity, and tooling around account handling. For a modern DApp and small frontend bundle, Ethers. js often reduces friction. Example: if you want simple read-only calls and clean signer flow with MetaMask, Ethers. js lets you request accounts and get a signer with fewer steps. Takeaway: choose the library that fits your project's size and developer ergonomics, but learn the provider and signer concepts—they are shared across both libraries.

keyIdea.title: Choose by ergonomics
keyIdea.text: Both libraries enable the same interactions; prefer Ethers.js for smaller bundles and clearer signer workflows when possible.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Web3.js vs Ethers.js
Comparison
API & Ergonomics
Ethers.js uses promise-first patterns and a compact API suitable for modern frontends.
Bundle Size
Ethers.js commonly yields smaller production bundles than Web3.js, which can matter for web performance.
Maturity & Features
Web3.js has a long history and broad examples, but both libraries support providers, signers, and events.
Concrete example (Ethers.js)
// Create a provider and signer with Ethers.js
import { ethers } from "ethers";
const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
const signer = await provider.getSigner();
const contract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signer);
This pattern is idiomatic in Ethers.js: provider for reads, signer for transactions.
Misconception
Bundle choice alone doesn't prevent runtime errors; you still need correct ABI and address, and the right signer or provider at call time.

screens.title: Providers and MetaMask
screens.subtitle: How a DApp connects to the blockchain and requests accounts

narration.text: A provider is the gateway between your frontend and an Ethereum node. In browser DApps the most common provider is MetaMask, which injects a window. ethereum object that your code can use. The practical flow is: detect the provider, request accounts, create a provider instance with a library, and obtain a signer for transactions. For example, using Ethers. js you create a BrowserProvider from window. ethereum, then call eth_requestAccounts to ask the user for permission. A common error is not handling account changes: wallets can switch accounts or networks, so your DApp must listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged events and reinitialize provider, signer, and contract instances as needed. Another pitfall is assuming the provider signs transactions — it does not by itself; you must call getSigner to obtain a signing object. Concrete example: after provider creation, call await provider. send('eth_requestAccounts', []) to trigger MetaMask; await provider. getSigner() gives you the signer to attach to contract instances. Why it matters: without a properly requested account and signer, state-changing calls will fail, producing confusing errors for users. Reflect: what UI cues can you add to show the wallet connection state clearly to users?

keyIdea.title: Provider lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Detect provider, request accounts, handle account/network changes, and obtain a signer for transactions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Providers & MetaMask
Connection Steps
  1. 1Detect window.ethereum and confirm a provider is available.
  2. 2Request accounts using eth_requestAccounts so the user can approve access.
  3. 3Create a provider instance in your library and call getSigner when you need to sign transactions.
  4. 4Listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged and reinitialize contract objects to avoid stale state.
Pro tip
Show connection status and a short account summary to reduce user confusion when MetaMask prompts appear.
Code example (Ethers.js)
// Connect to MetaMask and get a signer
import { ethers } from "ethers";
if (typeof window.ethereum !== 'undefined') {
  const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
  await provider.send('eth_requestAccounts', []);
  const signer = await provider.getSigner();
}
Common mistake
Calling contract methods that change state with a provider but without a signer causes an error saying the transaction requires a signer.
Why it matters
Proper account handling prevents painful UX around transaction failures and missing confirmations.

screens.title: Providers: MetaMask vs Hosted Nodes
screens.subtitle: When to use a browser wallet versus Infura or Alchemy

narration.text: There are two common provider patterns: browser wallets like MetaMask and hosted node services such as Infura or Alchemy. MetaMask is user-facing: it stores private keys and injects a provider into the browser so users can sign transactions locally. Hosted nodes provide RPC endpoints your server or frontend can query without a user wallet, useful for read-only data or server-initiated monitoring. The practical architecture often mixes both: use a hosted node to fetch background data or index events reliably, while relying on MetaMask for signed transactions initiated by a user. A misconception is to treat an RPC endpoint as a signer; it cannot sign for a user's account. Another common error is overloading a hosted node with subscription-heavy work that should be handled by an indexed service. Example: if you want to show global contract statistics in the UI without requiring a wallet, call Infura via provider and perform view calls. If you want to let a user change state, prompt them with MetaMask and obtain a signer. The key trade-offs are control of keys, reliability, rate limits, and UX. Ask yourself: which operations in your DApp must require the user to approve a signature, and which can be safely performed through a hosted node?

keyIdea.title: Provider trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Use hosted nodes for server-side reads and MetaMask for user-signed transactions; they complement one another in robust DApps.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Providers: MetaMask vs Hosted
Architecture Overview
MetaMask (Wallet)
Holds private keys in the browser and signs transactions for the user. Best for interactive, signed actions.
Infura / Alchemy (Hosted Node)
Provides a stable RPC endpoint for read-only calls, indexing, or server-side workflows without user keys.
Decision guide
  • •Use MetaMask when the user must approve and sign a transaction.
  • •Use Infura/Alchemy for background reads, indexing, and server-side event handling.
  • •Do not rely on hosted nodes for user signing; they cannot access private keys.
Example
A dashboard can use Infura to gather totals, while a button in the UI triggers MetaMask for a user-specific transfer.

screens.title: Instantiating a Contract in JavaScript
screens.subtitle: Using the contract address and ABI to create usable contract objects

narration.text: Instantiating a contract requires two exact pieces of information: the deployed contract address and its Application Binary Interface, or ABI. The address tells your code where the contract lives on chain, and the ABI describes the contract's public functions, events, and types so a library can encode and decode calls. With Ethers. js the process is straightforward: pass the address, ABI, and either a provider or signer to the Contract constructor. Use a provider for read-only calls and a signer when you need to send transactions. A practical example is a SimpleStorage contract: the ABI includes the storedData getter and the set setter. If you provide the wrong ABI or a different contract address, calls will either fail or return meaningless data—this is one of the most frequent runtime issues. When working from Remix, copy the compiled contract's ABI and the deployed address exactly. As a hands-on check, call a known view function immediately after instantiation and verify the result. Takeaway: contract instantiation is simple but brittle; treat address and ABI as authoritative and validate them before use. Instantiating a Contract in JavaScript means both are required and must match the deployed contract; mistakes here lead to decoding errors or failed calls.. In practical terms, using the contract address and abi to create usable contract objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Address + ABI
keyIdea.text: Both are required and must match the deployed contract; mistakes here lead to decoding errors or failed calls.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Instantiate Contract
What you need
  • Contract Address — the unique on-chain location, e.g., 0x... copied from deployment.
  • ABI — JSON array output from the Solidity compiler describing functions and events.
  • Provider or Signer — provider for reads, signer for transactions.
Check
After creating the instance, call a simple read-only function to verify instantiation succeeded.
Ethers.js example
import { ethers } from "ethers";
const provider = new ethers.BrowserProvider(window.ethereum);
const signer = await provider.getSigner();
const contractAddress = "0x..."; // deployed address
const contractABI = [ /* ABI array */ ];
const contract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signer);
const readOnly = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, provider);
Remember to use the signer-connected instance for state changes and the provider-connected instance for view calls.

screens.title: Calling view Functions (Read-only)
screens.subtitle: How to fetch data from a contract without gas or a signer

narration.text: View and pure functions are read-only operations that do not modify blockchain state; they can be executed without gas because they don't create a transaction. In a DApp you use a provider-connected contract instance for these calls. For example, if a SimpleStorage contract exposes storedData or a Counter exposes getCount, you call those functions and display the returned value directly. An important detail is value types: numeric values may be BigInt-like objects, so convert them to strings before rendering. A typical flow: instantiate a read-only contract with a provider, call the view method with await, and update your UI. Common mistakes include forgetting await, which yields a pending Promise, or using a signer-connected instance with no available account, which can cause confusion. Concrete example: await readOnlyContract. storedData() returns the stored value; call toString() for display. Another useful pattern is to schedule a short polling interval or listen for events so the UI stays current when transactions complete. Takeaway: use provider-bound contracts for reads, convert returned values safely for display, and always handle errors from the node or network gracefully. Calling view Functions (Read-only) means use provider-bound contracts to call view or pure functions; convert returned numeric values for safe display.. In practical terms, how to fetch data from a contract without gas or a signer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Read without gas
keyIdea.text: Use provider-bound contracts to call view or pure functions; convert returned numeric values for safe display.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Calling view Functions
Read pattern
// Provider-bound contract for read-only
const readOnlyContract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, provider);
const value = await readOnlyContract.getCount();
console.log('Count:', value.toString());
Handle return types and errors: convert BigNumber to string before display, and wrap calls in try/catch to show friendly messages if the node is unreachable.
Example
Call getCount on a deployed Counter contract and display the numeric string in the UI.
UI tips
  • Show a loading state while awaiting the view result.
  • Convert numeric returns safely for display with toString().
  • Use events or short polling to keep the UI in sync after transactions.
Common mistake
Forgetting await returns a Promise object, which often leads to wrong UI output like [object Promise].

screens.title: Sending Transactions and Signers
screens.subtitle: How to call state-changing functions, await receipts, and handle gas

narration.text: State-changing functions modify blockchain state and require a signed transaction plus gas. To perform a state change you'll use a contract instance connected to a signer. The practical sequence is: ensure a signer is available, call the function on the signer-bound contract, await the transaction response, and then await tx. wait() to receive the mined receipt. Example: calling contract. set(123) returns a transaction object; awaiting tx. wait() blocks until it is mined. Transactions can fail for many reasons: insufficient gas, reverted require statements inside the contract, or user cancellation in MetaMask. Libraries estimate gas automatically in many cases, but complex transactions may need manual overrides. Handle errors with try/catch, and inform the user about the confirmation flow in the wallet. A common misconception is that immediate reads after sending a transaction will reflect the new state; because mining takes time, you typically await the receipt or listen for an event that confirms the change. Example pattern: show a pending confirmation status, await tx. wait(), then refresh the read-only value or handle an event. Takeaway: treat transactions as asynchronous state transitions with multiple network steps and inform your user at each stage.

keyIdea.title: Transactions are asynchronous
keyIdea.text: Use a signer-bound contract, await tx and tx.wait(), and communicate pending / confirmed states to the user.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Sending Transactions
Transaction example
try {
  const tx = await contract.set(123); // signer-bound contract
  // Inform the user: transaction submitted
  const receipt = await tx.wait(); // wait for mining
  // Refresh read state or respond to event
} catch (error) {
  // Handle user rejection, revert, or gas error
}
Always present a clear pending/confirmed UI and catch errors from the wallet or node. Use receipt.status to check final success where applicable.
Gas & estimation
Libraries estimate gas, but complex contracts or interactions with other contracts can lead to underestimation. If a transaction keeps failing, examine require statements in the contract, check provided parameters, and consider manual gas limits as a last resort.
Common error
Using a provider-bound contract to send a transaction results in an error because the provider cannot sign the transaction for the user's account.

screens.title: Listening for Events
screens.subtitle: Reacting to contract-emitted events to update the UI

narration.text: Events are a lightweight way for contracts to emit logs that frontends can listen to. Rather than polling the chain repeatedly, you can subscribe to an event and react when it happens. For example, a Counter contract might emit a DataChanged(oldValue, newValue) event when the count changes. In the frontend, attach a listener with contract. on('DataChanged', (oldValue, newValue, event) => {... }) and update your UI inside that callback. Events are not stored as contract state — they are logs indexed by the node — and you should still verify finality if your application is sensitive to reorgs. A misconception is thinking events replace reading state; they are complements: events notify you that something happened, but a subsequent read verifies the latest state. Another practical tip is to deregister listeners when a component unmounts or when accounts change to avoid duplicate handlers. Example: after sending a transaction and receiving the receipt, you can also listen for the emitted event to update local state in near-real time. Takeaway: events reduce load and create responsive UIs, but always pair them with safe reads and lifecycle management.

keyIdea.title: Events for responsiveness
keyIdea.text: Subscribe to contract events to update UI without polling, and pair events with reads to confirm state.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Listening for Events
Event listener example
// Listen for DataChanged(oldValue, newValue)
contract.on('DataChanged', (oldValue, newValue, event) => {
  console.log('Data changed:', oldValue.toString(), newValue.toString());
  // Optionally re-read the latest state or update UI directly
});
Remove listeners when no longer needed to avoid duplicates: contract.off('DataChanged', handler).
Best practices
  • Use events to drive UI updates but confirm with a read for critical state.
  • Handle reorgs or delayed confirmations depending on application sensitivity.
  • Clean up listeners on account or network change to avoid stale handlers.
Concrete scenario
A token transfer emits Transfer events that let wallets and UIs update balances without frequent polling.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging
screens.subtitle: Frequent errors when interacting with contracts and how to fix them

narration.text: When integrating contracts into a frontend, a handful of mistakes appear repeatedly. First, using the wrong ABI or address: this leads to decoding failures or calls to a contract with different logic. Always copy the ABI and address from the exact deployed artifact. Second, missing await on promises: asynchronous calls return Promises and forgetting await produces visible Promise objects in the UI. Third, not using a signer for state-changing functions: sending a transaction through a provider without a signer causes an immediate error — understand the provider versus signer distinction. Fourth, incorrect gas estimation or not handling reverts: wrap transactions in try/catch and surface helpful messages. Fifth, failing to handle account and network changes leads to stale signer instances; listen for accountsChanged and chainChanged, then reinitialize your provider, signer, and contract. For debugging, log the ABI, address, and network chain ID before calling functions and check transaction receipts for revert reasons. Concrete example: if contract. set fails with a revert, examine require conditions in contract code and verify input parameters from the UI. Takeaway: structure your code to validate inputs, show clear user messages for wallet prompts, and reinitialize state when the underlying account or network changes.

keyIdea.title: Validate and catch
keyIdea.text: Always validate ABI and address, await promises, use a signer for transactions, and handle account/network changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Common Mistakes
Checklist
  • Confirm contract address and ABI match deployment.
  • Await asynchronous calls and show loading state.
  • Use a signer for transactions; provider for reads.
  • Catch errors and display friendly messages for wallet rejections or reverts.
Debugging tips
Log the contract address, ABI length, and network chain ID before calling. Inspect transaction receipts and revert reasons. Reproduce steps in a controlled environment like Remix's JavaScript VM to confirm contract logic.
If you see unexpected revert errors, verify function inputs and contract require statements rather than changing gas blindly.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Counter DApp Steps
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step checklist to implement, test, and observe transactions

narration.text: This activity checklist walks you through building and testing the Counter DApp. Step one: deploy the Counter contract in Remix and copy the deployed address and ABI. Step two: create an index. html with the provided starter scaffold and paste the address and ABI into the placeholders. Step three: detect MetaMask, request accounts, and obtain a signer. Step four: instantiate two contract objects—one provider-bound for reads, one signer-bound for writes. Step five: implement updateCount that calls getCount and displays the converted string. Step six: implement increment and decrement handlers that call the corresponding contract methods, await tx. wait(), and refresh the count. Step seven: add error handling and UI messages for pending and failed transactions. Step eight: add an event listener for the contract's change event to update the UI without polling. A common oversight during testing is forgetting to switch to the same network that the contract is deployed on. As you test, verify transaction hashes and receipts and use the console to inspect return values. After completing these steps, reflect on where to add defensive checks and how to surface friendly guidance for users when a transaction is rejected.

keyIdea.text: Deploy, copy address/ABI, connect wallet, instantiate provider/signer contracts, implement read and write functions, and add events and error handling.

narration.text: These are the foundational concepts you should retain. A provider connects your DApp to an Ethereum node and can be injected by a browser wallet like MetaMask or provided by a hosted service like Infura. A signer is the object capable of signing transactions and is typically derived from a provider after the user approves account access. The contract address locates a deployed contract on-chain, and the ABI describes the contract's public interface so your library can encode and decode function calls and events. Understanding these definitions and how they relate is crucial: provider gives access, signer gives permission, address gives location, and ABI gives meaning. Keep these terms clear as you implement a DApp to avoid common runtime errors. Key Concepts — Part 1 means provider, signer, contract address, and abi are the minimal vocabulary for interacting with smart contracts from a frontend.. In practical terms, essential terms to remember. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Essential definitions
keyIdea.text: Provider, signer, contract address, and ABI are the minimal vocabulary for interacting with smart contracts from a frontend.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
Provider
Connects your DApp to an Ethereum node (MetaMask, Infura).
Signer
An account capable of signing transactions, usually from a wallet.
ABI
JSON that describes contract functions, events, and types for external calls.
Summary

Remember the flow: provider gives access, signer grants permission, ABI defines the interface, and address locates the contract.

narration.text: Keep these practical reminders at hand as you code. Use a provider-bound contract for view or pure functions to avoid unnecessary signing and gas. Use a signer-bound contract for functions that change state and always await both the transaction submission and the mining receipt. Listen for contract events to update the UI in real time without aggressive polling, but pair event updates with a read to confirm state. Finally, validate that the ABI and deployed address match the contract you intend to call; incorrect values are the top source of runtime decoding errors. These concise patterns reduce friction when building DApps and improve user experience in production workflows. Key Concepts — Part 2 means provider for reads, signer for writes, await tx.wait(), listen for events, and validate abi/address to avoid decoding errors.. In practical terms, practical patterns and reminders. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.4 › What to Remember
Calls vs Transactions
Read-only calls are free. Transactions require signing and gas.
Await & Confirm
Await tx and tx.wait() and surface pending/confirmed states to the user.
Events
Use events to update UIs efficiently, but always verify state with a read when necessary.
Final takeaway

Mastering provider and signer lifecycles, correct instantiation, and clear user messaging is what turns a deployed contract into a usable DApp.
